CONGRANT.TITLE: Effect of Climate-induced Extreme Temperature on Rail Network Safety
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: Temperature is one of the major factors related to the buckling of railway tracks. Due to the increase in frequency and intensity of heat waves in recent years, there is a need to study the effect of climate-induced extreme temperature events on the vulnerability of the rail infrastructure to buckling. The proposed project aims to address that need with an interconnected methodology that combines structural analysis and network-level vulnerability assessment. The findings of this project are expected to support decision-making to allocate funds for rehabilitation projects of vulnerable tracks and new construction to support high-risk routes. The project will be performed by a team of researchers at the University Transportation Center for Railway Safety (UTCRS) at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV). The proposed budget for the project is $100,000. The timeline is expected to require 11 months.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Strategies and Technologies for Warning, Detection, and Prevention of Trespassing in the Vicinity of Highway-Rail Grade Crossings: State of the Practice and Research Needs
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The U.S. rail network is the largest, safest, and most efficient rail network in the world that operates over 160,000 rail miles. It plays a pivotal role in enabling the transportation of goods and people throughout the nation; and due to this crucial function, it serves as a fundamental pillar in supporting the economic expansion of the United States (Federal Railroad Administration, 2023). Simultaneously, the U.S. highway network plays a crucial role in enabling the seamless transportation of both individuals and cargo, consisting of a sophisticated linked grid of roads that spans the entire nation. According to data from the U.S. Department of Transportation (USDOT), the average monthly traffic volume for the year 2022 exceeded 3,000 billion miles. However, at the intersection of these two crucial transportation modes lies a point of concern—the Highway Rail Grade Crossing (HRGC).
HRGCs are where a road or pathway intersects with a railway track. These crossings facilitate the safe passage of vehicles, cyclists, and pedestrians across railway lines. However, if road users fail to notice warning signals and attempt to cross the tracks when a train is approaching, a catastrophic collision can occur, leading to severe injuries or fatalities. As such, HRGCs are a critical cause of hazardous conditions that may involve collisions between trains and vehicles or pedestrians. Thousands of highway-rail incidents occur in the US every year. Such incidents include many fatal crashes. Between 2010 and 2018, a total of 1,114 fatal crashes tragically occurred at HRGCs in the United States that resulted in the loss of 1,306 lives.
Trespassing at-or-near HRGC is a major safety issue. Trespassers are most often pedestrians trying to take a shortcut and/or do not notice incoming trains. Although it is illegal, more than 400 rail trespass fatalities occur every year. Various technologies and practices have been proposed to detect trespassing at rail crossings. Such technologies can involve various types of sensors such as radar, laser, infrared, magnetic, and many others. Such technologies can be infrastructure-based, locomotive-based, or a combination of both. Some innovative technologies include CCTV cameras assisted by computer vision, depth-sensing cameras, stereo vision, laser systems, and smart sensors enabled by deep learning, among others. Naturally, various technologies and practices come with diverse considerations, including aspects like their reliability, cost-effectiveness, accuracy, and smooth integration into rail infrastructure systems. There is a need to explore the advantages and disadvantages of existing and emerging technologies considering the needs and challenges of the rail infrastructure. The outcomes of this exploratory investigation guide decision-making and future research to prevent trespassing at HRGCs and improve the safety of the U.S. rail network.
